## Introduction
The standard meta-d' model assumes that participants have the same metacognitive sensitivity for both type 1 responses. As noted by @maniscalco2014, this assumption can be relaxed to allow different metacognitive sensitivities for each of the two type 1 responses in a variant of the meta-d' model known as the response-specific meta-d' model. @maniscalco2014 showed that the response-specific meta-d' model is much better suited for predicting the asymmetric ROCs generated by the unequal variance gaussian signal detection model (though, see `vignette('alternative_distributions')` for another approach to modeling asymmetric ROCs).

The response-specific meta-d' model is parameterized in the same way as the standard meta-d' model, except with separate type 2 parameters for each type 1 response. Specifically, now the type 2 evidence is distributed as follows:

$$
x_2 \sim \begin{cases}
\mathcal{D}_S^{(-\infty, \textrm{meta-}c_0]}\left(\textrm{meta-}d'_0\right) & \textrm{if } R=0 \\
\mathcal{D}_S^{[\textrm{meta-}c_1, \infty)}\left(\textrm{meta-}d'_1\right) & \textrm{if } R=1
\end{cases}
$$

This leads to analogous type 2 response probabilities as with the standard meta-d' model, only using the response-specific values $\textrm{meta-}d'_0$, $\textrm{meta-}d'_1$, $\textrm{meta-}c_0$, and $\textrm{meta-}c_1$:

$$
\begin{align*}
    P(C=c \;\vert\; R=r,S=s) &= \begin{cases}
    \frac{F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_0\right) -
    F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,1}^0\right)}
    {F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_0\right)}
    & \textrm{if } r=0, c=1 \\
    
    \frac{F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,k}^0\right) -
    F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,k+1}^0\right)}
    {F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_0\right)}  
    & \textrm{if } r=0, 1 \le c \le K \\
    
    \frac{F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,K}^0\right)}
    {F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_0)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_0\right)}
    & \textrm{if } r=0, c = K \\
    
    \frac{F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,1}^1\right) -
    F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_1 \right)}
    {1 - F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_1\right)}
    & \textrm{if } r=1, c=1 \\
    
    \frac{F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,k+1}^1\right) -
    F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,k}^1\right)}
    {1 - F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_1\right)}
    & \textrm{if } r=1, 1 \le c \le K \\
    
    \frac{1 - F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_{2,K}^1 \right)}
    {1 - F_{\mathcal{D}_s(\textrm{meta-}d'_1)}\left(\textrm{meta-}c_1\right)}
    & \textrm{if } r=1, c = K
    \end{cases}
\end{align*}
$$

The model is parameterized similarly, only with two separate $M$-ratios, $M_0 = \frac{\textrm{meta-}d'_0}{d'}$ and $M_1 = \frac{\textrm{meta-}d'_1}{d'}$. In `R`, the main parameter of the model is `M_1`, and `M_0` is represented by the parameter `Mzero`.


## Model fitting

To demonstrate how to fit the response-specific meta-d' model, we first load necessary packages in `R`:
```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(tidybayes)
library(hmetad)
```

We can simulate data from the response-specific meta-d' model using the function `sim_metad`, specifying separate values of $M$-ratio for each type 1 response and using the argument `response_specific=TRUE`:

```{r sim_metad_rs}
d <- sim_metad(100000, M_0=0.5, M_1=1.5, response_specific=TRUE)
d
```

First, we'll fit the standard meta-d' model assuming equal metacognitive sensitivities for the two responses:
```{r fit_metad}
m <- fit_metad(
    N ~ 1, d, prior=set_prior("std_normal()", class="Intercept")
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
m
```

Already from the model summary, we can see that the estimated $M$-ratio of approximately one (zero on the logarithmic scale) does not represent the data-generating $M$-ratios for either response. Instead, it is the average of the two $M$-ratios.

To fix this problem, now we'll fit the response-specific model by using the additional argument `response_specific=TRUE` and by providing corresponding formulas and priors for the new parameter `Mzero`:
```{r fit_metad_rs}
m_rs <- fit_metad(
    bf(N ~ 1, Mzero ~ 1),
    d, response_specific=TRUE,
    prior=set_prior("std_normal()", class="Intercept") +
        set_prior("std_normal()", class="Intercept", dpar="Mzero")
)
```
```{r, echo=FALSE}
m_rs
```

Now we see that the two estimated $M$-ratios reflect their true values.

## Model estimates

All of the post-processing functions in `hmetad` work in the same way for the response-specific meta-d' model. For example, here we gather posterior draws of the pseudo-type 1 ROC curves:

```{r roc1_draws}
newdata <- tibble(.row=1)

draws.roc1 <- bind_rows(
    roc1_rvars(m, newdata) |> mutate(model='Standard'),
    roc1_rvars(m_rs, newdata) |> mutate(model='Response-Specific')
)
```

Then, we can compare these estimates against the data:

```{r plot_roc1_draws}
draws.roc1 |>
    median_qi(p_hit, p_fa) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = p_fa, xmin = p_fa.lower, xmax = p_fa.upper,
        y = p_hit, ymin = p_hit.lower, ymax = p_hit.upper,
        linetype = model
    )) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_errorbar(orientation = "y", width = .01) +
    geom_errorbar(orientation = "x", width = .01) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(aes(x = p_fa, y = p_hit), data = roc1(d), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = 0:1, ylim = 0:1, expand = FALSE) +
    xlab("P(False Alarm)") +
    ylab("P(Hit)") +
    theme_bw(18)
```

From this plot, it is apparent that the standard meta-d' model under-predicts sensitivity for the `"1"` responses (left side of the curve) and over-predicts sensitivity for the `"0"` responses (right side of the curve). In contrast, here the response-specific model properly recovers the correct response probabilities.


Similarly, we can obtain posterior estimates of the type 2 ROC curves:
```{r roc2_draws}
draws.roc2 <- bind_rows(
    roc2_rvars(m, newdata) |> mutate(model='Standard'),
    roc2_rvars(m_rs, newdata) |> mutate(model='Response-Specific')
)
```

Again, we can compare these estimates against the data:

```{r plot_roc2_draws}
draws.roc2 |>
    median_qi(p_hit2, p_fa2) |>
    mutate(response = factor(response)) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = p_fa2, xmin = p_fa2.lower, xmax = p_fa2.upper,
        y = p_hit2, ymin = p_hit2.lower, ymax = p_hit2.upper,
        color = response, linetype = model
    )) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_errorbar(orientation = "y", width = .01) +
    geom_errorbar(orientation = "x", width = .01) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point(aes(x = p_fa2, y = p_hit2, color = response),
               data = mutate(roc2(d), response = factor(response)), inherit.aes = FALSE
               ) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = 0:1, ylim = 0:1, expand = FALSE) +
    xlab("P(Type 2 False Alarm)") +
    ylab("P(Type 2 Hit)") +
    theme_bw(18)
```

The type 2 ROC curves make apparent that, in this case, there are two different metacognitive sensitivities for the two type 1 responses. Additionally, while the standard model incorrectly assumes equal metacognitive sensitivity across type 1 responses, the response-specific model correctly infers that metacognitive sensitivity is higher for `"1"` responses than `"0"` responses.



## Conclusions
In cases where it is reasonable to assume that participants may have different metacognitive insight depending on which type 1 response they made, the response-specific meta-d' model is a useful tool for recovering this pattern. In the `hmetad` package, using the response-specific model is as simple as setting the argument `response_specific=TRUE`.
